title: CQRS and read models: projections that survive crashes
description: Split Library Loans into a write model (the lesson-8 aggregate over an event log) and a read model built by a projector; measure the consistency window, crash the projector, and make it checkpointed and idempotent.
outcome: You can build a projection with a checkpoint, measure how far it lags, detect drift, rebuild it, and make it survive a crash without losing or double-counting events.
environment: Python 3.12 standard library only (validated on 3.12.15 / Linux); unittest. Targets: Apple-silicon Mac mini (zsh) and Windows 11 PC (PowerShell); no new packages beyond L100.
overview: Commands go to the Member aggregate and append events; a projector thread turns events into a query table and logs `lag_ms` as JSON lines.
The base projector works until it is killed between saving its checkpoint and applying the event; then the view silently loses an event.

glossary.meaning: Query-shaped tables built only from events; disposable.
The last event seq a projector has applied, stored with the view.
Time from a committed event to it being visible in the read model.
Rows where the live view differs from a fresh rebuild.

concepts: Commands change the aggregate; queries read a separate, eventually consistent view.
View change + checkpoint in one transaction; idempotent handlers tolerate replays.
A read model can always be rebuilt from the event log; drift checks prove it.

codeWalkthrough.title: `READ_SCHEMA`: member_loans, book_status, checkpoint
codeWalkthrough.detail: The read model has its own database; the checkpoint table lives next to the rows it describes.

codeWalkthrough.title: `position()`
codeWalkthrough.detail: Where a (re)started projector resumes: events with seq > checkpoint.

codeWalkthrough.title: `self._save_checkpoint(seq)` before `apply`
codeWalkthrough.detail: The weakness: two transactions, and the position moves first. A crash in between skips the event.

codeWalkthrough.title: `active = active + ?`
codeWalkthrough.detail: Not idempotent: replaying an event counts it twice. The fix recounts from book_status.

codeWalkthrough.title: `lag_ms` in the JSON log
codeWalkthrough.detail: Now minus the event's recorded_at: the measured consistency window.

codeWalkthrough.title: `rebuild()`
codeWalkthrough.detail: Delete the rows and the checkpoint, replay from seq 0. The log is the truth; the view is disposable.

codeWalkthrough.title: `drift()`
codeWalkthrough.detail: Rebuild into a scratch database and diff row by row: the check you run after an incident or in a nightly job.

title: Resilience patterns: timeouts, circuit breaker, bulkhead, fallback
description: Wrap Library Loans' flaky catalogue dependency in a timeout, a circuit breaker and a fallback; then watch one slow dependency starve a shared thread pool and isolate it with a bulkhead.
outcome: You can explain and configure closed/open/half-open, read breaker and pool logs, and size per-dependency bulkheads so one slow service cannot take down the others.
environment: Python 3.12 standard library only (validated on 3.12.15 / Linux); unittest. Targets: Apple-silicon Mac mini (zsh) and Windows 11 PC (PowerShell); no new packages beyond L100. Uses threading and concurrent.futures.
overview: Borrowing needs members (required) and the catalogue title (nice to have, fallback allowed); every outbound call has a 0.1 s timeout.
The breaker logs its transitions as JSON lines; each request in the failure lab logs ok, error and pool usage.

glossary.meaning: Stops calling a failing dependency for a while (open), then tries one call (half-open).
A separate, bounded pool per dependency; excess calls are rejected, not queued.
A degraded answer for expected dependency errors.
All workers wait on one slow call; healthy work queues behind them.

concepts: A timeout frees the caller, not the thread doing the work.
A breaker stops hammering a sick dependency; it does not give threads back.
Bulkheads contain a slow dependency; fallbacks only for nice-to-have data.

codeWalkthrough.title: `future.result(timeout=timeout)` + `future.cancel()`
codeWalkthrough.detail: The caller stops waiting; cancel() only works if the call never started, so the worker stays busy.

codeWalkthrough.title: `Pool.busy` gauge
codeWalkthrough.detail: Counts running calls; `8/8` in a log line is the starvation signal.

codeWalkthrough.title: `Bulkhead.call`: `acquire(blocking=False)`
codeWalkthrough.detail: Reject at once (BulkheadFull) instead of queueing behind stuck calls.

codeWalkthrough.title: `Bulkhead._run`: `release()` in `finally`
codeWalkthrough.detail: The slot frees when the worker finishes, not when the caller gives up - otherwise the bulkhead leaks.

codeWalkthrough.title: `CircuitBreaker._record`: window, `min_calls`, `failure_rate`
codeWalkthrough.detail: Count-based sliding window of 10; opens at >= 50 % failures after 5 calls (resilience4j uses 100 calls by default).

codeWalkthrough.title: `call()` in open / half_open
codeWalkthrough.detail: Open fails fast until open_s passes; half-open allows one trial call.

codeWalkthrough.title: `with_fallback`
codeWalkthrough.detail: Only TimeoutError, CircuitOpen, BulkheadFull, ConnectionError become a degraded answer; bugs still raise.

tradeOffs.costs: Threads still stuck; load keeps hitting a sick service

tradeOffs.gains: Fails fast, gives the dependency room to recover
tradeOffs.costs: Tuning (window, threshold, open time); no thread isolation
tradeOffs.chooseWhen: Dependency fails hard (errors) more than it slows

tradeOffs.gains: One slow dependency cannot starve others
tradeOffs.costs: More pools to size; rejects under bursts

inRealSystems: HTTP clients get per-host connection pools and timeouts; resilience4j/Polly add breakers and bulkheads around them.

useWhen: Use a breaker + bulkhead around every remote dependency whose slowness you cannot control; fall back only for optional data.

title: Consumer-driven contract testing
description: Library Loans (consumer) writes its expectations of the catalogue (provider) as a versioned contract generated from its own tests; the provider's build replays it. A renamed field breaks the provider build, not production.
outcome: You can generate a contract from consumer tests, verify a provider against it with provider states and type matchers, and explain what Pact and a broker add.
environment: Python 3.12 standard library only (validated on 3.12.15 / Linux); unittest. Targets: Apple-silicon Mac mini (zsh) and Windows 11 PC (PowerShell); no new packages beyond L100. CI only: pact-python==4.2.0 (requirements-ci.txt; needs Python >= 3.11).
overview: contract.py is a stdlib mini-Pact: mock provider from examples, a JSON contract in contracts/, a provider verifier with states.
The base verifier compares status codes only, so a renamed field passes every check until the real consumer calls it.

glossary.meaning: The provider's obligations, derived from what its consumers actually use.
Named test data the provider sets up before an interaction ('book b1 exists').
Any value of the same JSON type is accepted.
Pact Broker check: was this version verified against what is deployed?

concepts: Generate the contract from the consumer's real client, not by hand.
The provider verifies every consumer contract in its own build.
Match on shape and type; ignore extra fields (tolerant reader).

title: SLOs and error budgets: burn-rate alerts from request logs
description: Compute availability and latency SLIs from three days of structured request logs, turn SLOs into error budgets and multiwindow burn-rate alerts, and see an average hide a broken p99.
outcome: You can define an SLI as good/valid events from logs, compute burn rate and budget consumed, configure page/ticket alerts per the SRE Workbook, and let a local model word an incident summary whose numbers code checks.

code:
"""Architecture fitness functions as CI gates (lesson 16 lab code). Run: python fitness.py  (exit 1 = a gate failed)

Each gate prints one JSON line {"gate", "ok", "value", "budget"}. Same ideas as import-linter contracts,
k6 thresholds and pytest-benchmark comparisons. `--solution` runs the gates on solution/loans_repo.py.
"""
import argparse
import ast
import importlib.util
import json
import pathlib
import sys
import timeit

import loans_repo
from http_api import start
from load_test import run_load

HERE = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent
QUERY_BUDGET = 2  # SQL statements per report - for 10 AND 500 loans: the count must not grow with the data
BENCH_BUDGET_MS = 50  # generous on purpose: timing gates must not flake on a busy CI runner
P95_BUDGET_MS = 200
FORBIDDEN = {"domain.py": {"sqlite3", "http", "urllib", "loans_repo", "http_api"}}  # domain stays pure


class QueryCounter:
    """Counts the SQL statements SQLite actually executes (sqlite3 trace callback)."""

    def __init__(self, conn):
        self.conn, self.statements = conn, []

    def __enter__(self):
        self.conn.set_trace_callback(self.statements.append)
        return self

    def __exit__(self, *exc):
        self.conn.set_trace_callback(None)


def gate_import_boundaries(folder=HERE):
    found = []
    for file, forbidden in FORBIDDEN.items():
        tree = ast.parse((folder / file).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        names = ({a.name.split(".")[0] for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.Import) for a in n.names} |
                 {n.module.split(".")[0] for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.ImportFrom) and n.module})
        found += [f"{file} imports {name}" for name in sorted(names & forbidden)]
    return {"gate": "import-boundaries", "ok": not found, "value": found, "budget": "domain.py imports no adapters"}


def gate_query_count(repo):
    counts = {}
    for loans in (10, 500):
        conn = repo.seeded_db(loans=loans)
        with QueryCounter(conn) as counter:
            repo.overdue_report(conn)
        counts[loans] = len(counter.statements)  # deterministic: same data, same count, on every machine
    return {"gate": "query-count", "ok": max(counts.values()) <= QUERY_BUDGET, "value": counts, "budget": QUERY_BUDGET}


def gate_microbenchmark(repo):
    conn = repo.seeded_db(loans=500)
    runs = timeit.repeat(lambda: repo.overdue_report(conn), number=5, repeat=5)
    best_ms = min(runs) / 5 * 1000  # min() of the repeats: the least disturbed run (timeit docs)
    return {"gate": "micro-benchmark", "ok": best_ms <= BENCH_BUDGET_MS, "value": round(best_ms, 2),
            "budget": BENCH_BUDGET_MS}


def gate_response_time(repo):
    server, url = start(repo, loans=500)
    try:
        result = run_load(url + "/reports/overdue", users=4, requests_per_user=10)
    finally:
        server.shutdown()
        server.server_close()
    return {"gate": "response-time-p95", "ok": result["p95_ms"] <= P95_BUDGET_MS and result["errors"] == 0,
            "value": result, "budget": P95_BUDGET_MS}


def main(argv=None, out=sys.stdout):
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.splitlines()[0])
    parser.add_argument("--solution", action="store_true", help="check solution/loans_repo.py")
    repo = loans_repo
    if parser.parse_args(argv).solution:
        spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("loans_repo_solution", HERE / "solution" / "loans_repo.py")
        repo = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
        spec.loader.exec_module(repo)
    results = [gate_import_boundaries(), gate_query_count(repo), gate_microbenchmark(repo), gate_response_time(repo)]
    for result in results:
        print(json.dumps(result, sort_keys=True), file=out)
    failed = [r["gate"] for r in results if not r["ok"]]
    print("fitness: " + ("all gates passed" if not failed else "FAILED " + ", ".join(failed)), file=out)
    return 1 if failed else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
